transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been going on that brought you in today?

Hi, yeah. Thanks. Um, well, I guess what brings me in is that I’m just losing hours and hours every day to rechecking things. Like, I'll be checking my dressing supplies, or the door locks, or at work it's file dimensions and my revision notes... 

I'm an engineer, actually. I graduated recently and my first job has been, well, it's a lot of CAD work. My supervisor, Dave, he's incredibly particular about the layer naming conventions in the software. It actually really reminds me of my senior design professor who would literally fail you if the margins on your report were off by a millimeter. We used to stay up until 3 AM just drinking terrible vending machine coffee in the lab—which, by the way, I heard they finally replaced the machine in the engineering building, but my buddy told me it still tastes like burnt plastic. I don't know why they can't just get a decent espresso maker in there, you know? 

But, um... where was I? Right, the checking. Yeah, it's just... I don’t feel allowed to move on until I’ve gone through the exact same checking routine enough times. Like I have to keep checking the locks or the files until the anxiety finally drops. It just takes up so much of my day.

When you're checking things like the door locks or file dimensions, are you doing it because you have intrusive, upsetting thoughts that something bad will happen if you don't check them, or is it more that you just feel tense and worried about making mistakes?

Um, it's definitely the upsetting thoughts. It's not just regular worry. Like, even after I *know* I've reviewed a CAD file perfectly, this really loud thought just cuts in that I missed one tiny thing and it's going to turn into a massive design mistake that actually hurts someone. Which is terrifying, honestly. It reminds me of this documentary I watched about the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse—have you seen that? My roommate, Greg, put it on last weekend. He’s always watching those engineering disaster shows. He uses my streaming account, actually, because he refuses to pay for his own, which is kind of annoying since he makes way more money than I do working in finance. He leaves his unwashed protein shaker bottles all over our sink, too, and they smell awful if you leave them sitting. 

But, um... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, the thoughts. Yeah, I just can't reason it away. It happens with my physical stuff, too, like my dressing supplies. Even after I know I’ve completely cleaned the wound area, my brain is just screaming that I missed a microscopic spot and it’s going to turn into this horrible, dangerous infection. I actually buy my supplies at that pharmacy down on 4th street, and the pharmacist there has this really bizarre, booming laugh. I always try to avoid his line. I think he drives a bright yellow Mustang, I saw him getting out of it once in the parking lot and it had racing stripes... but yeah, the thoughts just don't stop. I can't just logic my way out of them.
When these upsetting thoughts come up, do you feel driven to perform certain behaviors or mental acts to reduce the anxiety or prevent something bad from happening?

Yeah, exactly. That's... that's actually what I was trying to say earlier. I feel completely driven to do it. Like, I'm losing hours and hours to rechecking things—the dressing supplies, the door locks, the file dimensions and revision notes at work. I just don't feel allowed to move on until I've gone through the exact same routine enough times that the anxiety finally drops. 

Take the door locks, for example. Our apartment door has this really sticky deadbolt, and my landlord, Mr. Henderson, keeps saying he's going to send a guy to fix it, but he never does. He's always claiming he's "busy" at his other property, which I know for a fact is just a duplex down by the river that flooded last year. It was actually on the local news because someone's kayak literally floated into the living room. Can you imagine dealing with water damage like that? Mold mitigation is incredibly expensive, and you have to rip out all the drywall, which is a nightmare because drywall dust gets into the HVAC system and then you're breathing it in for months... 

But, um... wait, I'm sorry, I lost my train of thought. What did you ask me? Oh, right, doing things to stop the anxiety. Yeah, I just have to do my checking routines over and over until the panic stops. I just don't feel like I have a choice.

The compulsions are not performed in response to a feared situation related to anxiety or trauma, ruling out other candidates such as F41.0, F43.22, and F40.21.

No definitive exclusion yet.
